subject: Account for country-level predictors and individual-level predictors in a mixed model?

messages.author: 13197907c14ddd25
messages.subject: Account for country-level predictors and individual-level predictors in a mixed model?
parts:
Dear list,

I'm having a bit of trouble with building a relatively simple mixed model in Stan. I'm using a binomial logit model, to explain what basically comes down to the number of heads resulting from a known number of coin tosses, where coins are tossed in different countries, with a fixed number of sessions of coin tosses within each country (i.e. a few sessions that each have a known number of coin tosses). I have two types of predictors; the first set varies within countries, while the second set only varies between countries (i.e. they capture a characteristic of the country). 

I'm using the model below to capture these differences and this produces reasonable estimates and fairly accurate predictions. Nevertheless, I wonder if I correctly account for the different types of predictors when I allow the country-level predictors to affect the overall intercept that is used as the mean for the country-level random intercepts. Could it be that I am overestimating my confidence in the country-level effects because the country-level predictors are still an Ntotal x Npredictors_c matrix, rather than a matrix that has only as many rows as there are countries (in which case I would probably also have to change beta0_c[country] into beta0_c)? Or would it be better to tackle this in a different way altogether?

All suggestions are most welcome. Thanks in advance!

data {
    int<lower = 0> Ntotal; // total number of sessions
    int<lower = 0> tosses[Ntotal]; // number of tosses for this session
    int<lower = 0> heads[Ntotal]; // number of heads in this session
    int<lower = 1> Ncountries;
    int<lower = 1, upper = Ncountries> country[Ntotal];
    int<lower = 0> Npredictors_i; // number of within-country predictors
    matrix[Ntotal, Npredictors_i] X_i; // within-country predictors
    int<lower = 0> Npredictors_c; // number of country-level predictors
    matrix[Ntotal, Npredictors_c] X_c; // country-level predictors
}

parameters {
    real mu0; // overall intercept
    real<lower = 0> sigma; // variability of country-level random intercepts
    vector[Ncountries] beta0_c; // country-level random intercepts, after accounting for between-country effects
    vector[Npredictors_c] country beta; //country-level effects
    vector[Npredictors_i] beta; // within-country effects
}

model {
    mu0 ~ normal(0, 1);
    sigma ~ cauchy(0, 1);
    beta ~ normal(0, 1);
    countrybeta ~ normal(0, 1);

    beta0_c[country] ~ normal(mu0 + X_c * countrybeta, sigma);
    heads ~ binomial_logit(tosses, beta0_c[country] + X_i * beta);
}

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Account for country-level predictors and individual-level predictors in a mixed model?
parts:
> On Aug 17, 2016, at 8:41 PM, Allard van Mossel <a.van....@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Dear list,
>
> I'm having a bit of trouble with building a relatively simple mixed model in Stan. I'm using a binomial logit model, to explain what basically comes down to the number of heads resulting from a known number of coin tosses, where coins are tossed in different countries, with a fixed number of sessions of coin tosses within each country (i.e. a few sessions that each have a known number of coin tosses).

We prefer the general term "binary trial" to "coin toss" as these
aren't coin tosses.

> I have two types of predictors; the first set varies within countries, while the second set only varies between countries (i.e. they capture a characteristic of the country).
>

> I'm using the model below to capture these differences and this produces reasonable estimates and fairly accurate predictions. Nevertheless, I wonder if I correctly account for the different types of predictors when I allows the country-level predictors to affect the overall intercept that is used as the mean for the country-level random intercepts. Are there any alternatives?

>
> Thanks in advance!
>
> data {
> int<lower = 0> Ntotal; // total number of sessions
> int<lower = 0> tosses[Ntotal]; // number of tosses for this session
> int<lower = 0> heads[Ntotal]; // number of heads in this session

I'd strongly suggest more meaningful variable names
than "tosses" and "heads".

> int<lower = 1> Ncountries;
> int<lower = 1, upper = Ncountries> country[Ntotal];
> int<lower = 0> Npredictors_i; // number of within-country predictors
> matrix[Ntotal, Npredictors_i] X_i; // within-country predictors

> int<lower = 0> Npredictors_c; // number of country-level predictors
> matrix[Ntotal, Npredictors_c] X_c; // country-level predictors

You just want Npredictors_c here and to make it a vector. See
below for why this is most likely wrong.

> }
>
> parameters {
> real mu0; // overall intercept
> real<lower = 0> sigma; // variability of country-level random intercepts
> vector[Ncountries] beta0_c; // country-level random intercepts, after accounting for between-country effects
> vector[Npredictors_c] country beta; //country-level effects

I think this is supposed to be countrybeta. It helps immensely
if you send us models that compile.

> vector[Npredictors_i] beta; // within-country effects
> }
>
> model {
> mu0 ~ normal(0, 1);
> sigma ~ cauchy(0, 1);
> beta ~ normal(0, 1);
> countrybeta ~ normal(0, 1);
>
> beta0_c[country] ~ normal(mu0 + X_c * countrybeta, sigma);

This last line is almost certainly wrong. It's not guaranteed to
put a distribution on each instance of beta0_c and may put more
than one on some.

I think you want something like the following:

data {
vector[Npredictors_c] X_c; // predictors for countries

and then the parameters will look like:

parameters {
real beta_c; // country slope
real mu_c; // country intercept

and the delaration for beta0_c is as you have it, with the model
for them being:

model {
beta0_c ~ normal(beta_c * X_c + mu_c, sigma);
> heads ~ binomial_logit(tosses, beta0_c[country] + X_i * beta);

Aside from naming, the likeihood here looks like what you want.

You will probably find it more efficient (and much better converging)
to use the non-centered parameterization, but lets take one
step at a time.

There's a good discussion of these kinds of models in Andrew's
papers on red-state/blue-state (recreated in the Gelman and Hill
regression book, which I'd strongly recommend if you're working
on these kinds of problems).

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Account for country-level predictors and individual-level predictors in a mixed model?
parts:
Dear Bob,

Thank you for your time and the quick response!

>     matrix[Ntotal, Npredictors_c] X_c; // country-level predictors 

You just want Npredictors_c here and to make it a vector.  See 
below for why this is most likely wrong.

>     beta0_c[country] ~ normal(mu0 + X_c * countrybeta, sigma); 

This last line is almost certainly wrong.  It's not guaranteed to 
put a distribution on each instance of beta0_c and may put more 
than one on some.   

I think you want something like the following: 

  data { 
    vector[Npredictors_c] X_c;  // predictors for countries 

and then the parameters will look like: 

  parameters { 
    real beta_c;  // country slope 
    real mu_c;    // country intercept 

and the delaration for beta0_c is as you have it, with the model 
for them being: 

  model { 
    beta0_c ~ normal(beta_c * X_c + mu_c, sigma);

Thanks for pointing this out, that line is indeed wrong. However, I have either misunderstood how Stan uses the specification of a model, or my ambiguous naming (sorry about that, I will be more clear in the future) might have lead to a bit of confusion.
If I follow the suggestion above, my understanding is that I will have one parameter for a country slope (`beta_c`), that is the same for every country. I do indeed want the same slopes for each country predictor variable, but since I have multiple country-level predictor variables (`Npredictors_c` predictor variables, such as GDP, and other socio-economic factors) I think I should adapt the model slightly to fit a separate country slope for each of them. I would also have the change the format of the `X_c` data to reflect that I have one observation for each predictor variable, for each country.

The model would then be as follows:

data {
    int<lower = 0> Ntotal;                              // total number of sessions
    int<lower = 0> tosses[Ntotal];                      // number of tosses for this session
    int<lower = 0> heads[Ntotal];                       // number of heads in this session

int<lower = 1> Ncountries;                          // number of countries    
    int<lower = 1, upper = Ncountries> country[Ntotal]; // indicates the country of the session
    int<lower = 0> Npredictors_i;                       // number of regular predictor variables
    matrix[Ntotal, Npredictors_i] X_i;                  // regular predictors
    int<lower = 0> Npredictors_c;                       // number of country-level predictor variables
//OLD:    matrix[Ntotal, Npredictors_c] X_c;
    matrix[Ncountries, Npredictors_c] X_c;              // country-level predictors (one entry for each predictor, for each country)

}

parameters {
    real mu0;                           // overall intercept
    real<lower = 0> sigma;              // variability of country-level random intercepts

vector[Ncountries] beta0_c;         // country-level intercepts, after accounting for country-level predictors
    vector[Npredictors_c] countrybeta;  // effect of country-level predictor variables
    vector[Npredictors_i] beta;         // effect of regular predictor variables

}

model {
    mu0 ~ normal(0, 1);
    sigma ~ cauchy(0, 1);
    beta ~ normal(0, 1);
    countrybeta ~ normal(0, 1);

//OLD:    beta0_c[country] ~ normal(mu0 + X_c * countrybeta, sigma);
    beta0_c ~ normal(mu0 + X_c * countrybeta, sigma);

heads ~ binomial_logit(tosses, beta0_c[country] + X_i * beta);
}

Your variable naming (`mu_c` and `beta_c`) is much more clear than mine and I will adopt this in my model—I'm just using the old naming here to ease the comparison with the old version of the model. The same goes for the non-centered parameterization (which turned out to be about twice as efficient, although Stan already does a great job). Gelman and Hill's book is very helpful, and this has gotten me to also buy Gelman's Bayesian book. I remember seeing those red-state/blue-state models featured on his blog a while ago. I looked them up and they're quite similar, although I couldn't find the Stan code, probably because this dates from before Stan?

- Allard

Yes, dates from before Stan. Gelman and Hill has the
red-state/blue-state example in it. The extra you get
there is a multivariate prior in that it's varying slope
and varying intercept (we now prefer different priors than
the hack of scaling a covariance matrix---we can put an
LKJ prior on a correlation matrix and scale that).

The Gelman et al. Bayesian Data Analysis book is *much*
harder in that it assumes much more mathematical skill and
background (I had to read Gelman and Hill first and I was
a math major who'd done analysis as an undergrad, but no stats).

- Bob
